meta.title: Who really said "By all means, marry. If you get a good wife, you'll become happy; if you get a bad one, you'll become a philosopher"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No ancient text has it — this famous Socrates marriage quip is a modern epigram first printed in the 1930s–50s, once even credited to Sydney Smith.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'By all means, marry. If you get a good wife, you'll become happy; if you get a bad one, you'll become a philosopher'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Socrates. The line appears in no ancient source; its earliest known printings are 20th-century joke collections, one crediting Sydney Smith.

answer.label: Not Socrates — a modern witticism
answer.sourceLine: This exact quip appears in none of the ancient sources for Socrates — not in Plato, Xenophon, or Diogenes Laërtius. It is a modern epigram of unknown authorship: the earliest known printings date only to the 1930s–1950s (a 1935 magazine, a 1949 book, and a 1955 handbook that instead credited the wit Sydney Smith), always with a bare “Socrates said” and never a real citation. The closest thing Socrates genuinely said about marriage is Diogenes Laërtius’ report that, asked whether one should marry, he answered “whichever you do you will repent it.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: By all means marry; if you get a good wife, you’ll become happy; if you get a bad one, you’ll become a philosopher.
trail: Wikiquote files this under “Misattributed” ↗, noting its origin is unknown and its earliest sightings are a 1935 magazine, a 1949 book, and a 1955 handbook — none citing an ancient source.
The 1955 Speaker’s Handbook of Epigrams and Witticisms assigned the line to Sydney Smith, not Socrates, showing compilers had no fixed attribution — per Wikiquote ↗.
Socrates’ only genuinely-documented marriage aphorism is the gloomier “whichever you do you will repent it ↗” in Diogenes Laërtius.
source.excerptNote: Widely circulated as Socrates, but appearing in no ancient text; a variant even names Socrates’ wife Xanthippe (“a common scold like my Xanthippe—why then you will become a philosopher”).
source.rightsNote: The wording’s true author is unknown: the earliest known appearances are 20th-century (from 1935 onward), and one credits Sydney Smith rather than Socrates. Because the origin of this specific phrasing cannot be tied to any identifiable pre-1931 work, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: About Socrates
author.metaLine: c. 470–399 BC · Athenian philosopher, teacher of Plato
author.bio: Socrates was an Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing himself; everything attributed to him is secondhand, through his pupils Plato and Xenophon and later compilers such as Diogenes Laërtius. His reputedly difficult marriage to Xanthippe became a stock comic theme in antiquity, which is exactly why later humorists found it so easy to hang marriage jokes on his name. Leaving no texts of his own, he remains one of history’s most misquoted figures.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-shared “Socrates” lines, but it is a modern joke retrofitted onto an ancient name. No text from antiquity contains it.

items.why: The polished “good wife → happy / bad wife → philosopher” formula is found in no ancient source. Wikiquote lists it under “Misattributed” with “origin unknown” ↗, tracing the earliest known printings only to a 1935 magazine, a 1949 book, and a 1955 handbook.

Herbert Prochnow’s Speaker’s Handbook of Epigrams and Witticisms (1955) attributed the line to the English wit Sydney Smith (1771–1845), not Socrates — a sign that even mid-century compilers had no settled source, as Wikiquote records ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: What Socrates is genuinely reported to have said about marriage is far bleaker: asked whether a man should marry, he replied “whichever you do you will repent it ↗” (Diogenes Laërtius, Lives II.33).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke works because it fits the ancient caricature of Socrates as a long-suffering husband. Diogenes Laërtius and Xenophon both dwell on his difficult wife Xanthippe, and Socrates is portrayed as claiming he chose so spirited a partner deliberately — if he could tolerate her, he could get along with anyone. That reputation made him an irresistible magnet for a marriage wisecrack he never actually made.

The modern epigram compresses that lore into a tidy dilemma, but the tidiness is the tell: genuine Socratic sayings survive only in ancient Greek texts, and this one surfaces first in 20th-century English joke collections.
context.pull: A modern punchline wearing an ancient toga.
